utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please. Do we have problems? Are you receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I appear for the Prosecution, together with my colleagues, Mr. Jose Doria, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Wubben wishes me to advise you that he's unable to be here this morning because he has a commitment in another case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones, appearing for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries before we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You know that we will be sitting right through to 11, rather than have a break at 10.30. We'll work until 11, saving any request from the technicians for a short break to change tapes, if necessary. At 11, we need to stop, because I have a personal matter that I have to attend to. You could please -- could you please bring in the witness. We don't need to go into private session for the time being, no? Because the curtains are drawn in our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, sir, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will be proceeding with your direct, with the examination-in-chief. Do you think that you will finish today, Mr. Di Fazio? I suppose so, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The only thing that might take a little time with this witness is some of the documents towards the end of my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But I'll try and whip through those as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not hurrying. This is a witness who was mentioned in the -- who is a crucial witness, in any case, so I think we will need to give him our utmost attention, both Prosecution and Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And, unfortunately, and I hope this doesn't happen, but if, unfortunately, I haven't finished today, I am confident that we will have finished the lion's share, and it'll just be a matter of wrapping it up on the day after. But I'll do my best to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Witness C007, yesterday we got to the point where you had finished describing your arrival in Srebrenica, the beatings that you suffered at the police station, and your transfer to what was to be your place of incarceration for some months. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were being held in detention, after that -- I'm not sure what you have in mind. How long was I there for, or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, I'm just reminding you to the point to which we got, and now I'll ask the question that I want to put to you. You were incarcerated in this prison in Srebrenica. I want you now to tell the Trial Chamber the names, the personalities, who were inside the cell with you at the prison.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, yes, the persons were Branko Sekulic, Dragan Ilic, and the man from Kalabace, whose name escapes me right now. He was a soldier, and the name escapes me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You mentioned a gentleman yesterday who had been incarcerated with you in the stable who was taken with you, Jakov Dzokic. Was he also in the prison cell in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, that's true. I couldn't remember his name for a while there. Jakov Dzokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were there any men who you only know by nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the names of two persons, Mico and Kosta. I don't know their last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: About how old was Mico and about how old was Kosta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you only what I remember. I think they must have been about 40 or 50 years of age. I'm not sure if the two of them were the same age, or if one was younger and the other slightly older.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier you mentioned that there were two men -- sorry, I'll withdraw that. Earlier you mentioned that some of the inmates came from a place called Kalabace. Did Kosta or Mico come from Kalabace, or are you talking about other men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Dzokic was the only person from Kalabace.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you recall being informed or told where Mico came from or where Kosta came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people said that they were from Kravica, but I can't be certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you say "people said that they were from Kravica," is that something you learned after your release? Or are you talking about information you received while you were incarcerated, inside the prison cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was incarcerated, I heard the words "Mico" and" Kosta" being called out. I heard those names being called out. I'm not sure in relation to whom, but those names were called out among the people who were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. But did you ever hear from Kosta or Mico, did you ever hear from their mouths, that they were from a particular place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I don't know where they come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And what ethnicity were Kosta and Mico?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mico was an ethnic Serb, and Kosta as well. These are Serb names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the names you've told us about now, were there any inmates in the cell who were elderly men, older men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an old man, aged 60 or more. I don't know where from. And there was a deaf and dumb person, middle-aged. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know of a place in Bosnia called Zenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of the place but I've never been there, so I'm not sure about its exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you hear about the place while you were in custody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's where I heard about it, because there was a man from Zenica there. I heard that he was from Zenica, but I can't remember his first or last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You earlier described, just a short moment ago, an old man aged 60 or more. Is he the one from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know where that man was from, but I don't think he was from Zenica. Probably not. Actually, I can't be positive about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: During your stay in the prison, did you notice the presence of children at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a young boy, aged, perhaps, 8 or 10. He would come to see us. And he told us that the old man was actually his grandfather.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How often did you see this child?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three times. Perhaps more. I can't be sure now. Two or three times, that much is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Inside the cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I apologise for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. When you arrived in Srebrenica, did you have any personal identification with you; your papers, your documents, your ID card, driver's license, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had my ID, my military identification booklet, and I had the license for the rifle that I had from before the war. And all of these were taken from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Were they taken whilst in Srebrenica, or were they taken earlier when you were in the stable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica, once I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And just very briefly, you mentioned that you had a military identification booklet. What did that -- what is it? And when did you get that, and what does it relate to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's called a military identification booklet from the former JNA, the military service I did there. I had the military identification booklet, I had my ID, and the license for my rifle. Those are the things that I would usually carry whenever I went to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: From where -- from what year, what period of time, did the military identification booklet relate to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The booklet dates back to 1975 and 1976. That was when I did my compulsory military service, from 1975 on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll turn to another topic now. In the time that you were in the prison in Srebrenica, were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, people were being beaten. How much and who exactly, I really can't say. But we were beaten, that's certain. I still have a mark on my left shoulder blade and on my head, a sharp object, some sort of a sharp implement. Whether it was a knife or a bayonet, I really can't say. I only know that I still have a scar on my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, I'd like to take you through the beatings, and just answer the questions as briefly as you can and we can get through this faster. Firstly, just tell me this: Were you the only person subjected to beatings, or were all the other inmates that you have described so far also subjected to beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Others were also subjected to beatings, as well as myself. Whenever they came in to beat me, obviously, no one stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In effect, no one was spared.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one, not to the extent that I was able to see. I don't think anyone was spared.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We'll get to the period of your release from prison later. But from the time that you entered the prison in Srebrenica to the time you were taken away from the prison, was there ever any cessation in the beatings? In other words, did days or more significant periods of time ever pass when you were without being assaulted and attacked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this could only have happened when we were taken to the hospital. I'm not sure how many days they gave me. One, two, or three days, that was how long I remained at the hospital. But that was the period during which we were not beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. As a result of these beatings, did you and did the other inmates bleed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Everyone was bleeding, and everyone was black and blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We'll get into the details slowly. First of all, could you see blood on walls, the walls of your cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Could you see blood on the floor? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All over the place. On the floor. Depends on where each of us were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just answer my questions, if you can, with a yes or no at this stage. Could you see blood on the faces of your fellow inmates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Could you see blood on their clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Following the beatings, could you see signs of attack or assault on the faces of your fellow inmates? And by that I'm referring to things like cut lips or black eyes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, black eyes, swellings as a result of blows, swellings to the flesh. People had black eyes, blood on their faces. I can't say I remember any cuts specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the beatings occur during the day as well as the night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both day and night. I'm speaking about Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand that there was no electricity in Srebrenica at that time. How were the beatings conducted at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no electricity. They had candles, and they would light bits of paper wrapped around wooden sticks. They would light those, bring them inside, and use these bits of paper to watch us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber if, during the course of these beatings, whether you suffered loss of consciousness, and whether you saw your fellow inmates also suffer a loss of consciousness, following the attacks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, for one, certainly did, and most probably others also suffered loss of consciousness. Once they had been beaten, they would probably just fall down. I can speak about myself. I certainly was unconscious, and that's the reason I don't know many of the things that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber if instruments were used during these attacks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They used bludgeons or sticks that they would use to beat us. I, for one, was being kicked by a man who was wearing military boots. He would kick me in the chest and beat me, and I was not exactly fully aware of what was going on around me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were rifle butts used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I want to know something about the perpetrators of these attacks. Firstly, were any guards, guards in the prison, involved in the attacks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure who they were. Whether they were guards or what else, I really can't say. The man who beat me came frequently to beat me. I'm speaking about myself. I'm not sure if it was the same man who was beating the others too. As for the rest of them, I used to know one of them. Those were people who were rather young at the time. They could have been aged 20, 25, 30. They were quite young.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your last answer tends to imply that there was one person who beat you. Is that the case, or is it the case that you had -- you suffered beatings at the hands of more than one person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was this one man whom I met who beat me. But other people came in to beat me and beat the rest of us. Others would come in too. But the beatings were predominantly administered by this one man, the one who kicked me with his boots.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see if your assailants were dressed in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one who beat me was dressed predominantly in civilian clothes, but he did have the military boots. As for the rest, some had military uniforms and some didn't, and certainly not all of them were wearing uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You may or may not be able to remember this detail, but of the ones who were dressed in uniform, do you recall if they were also armed at the time that they carried out these attacks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that some carried weapons and some didn't. I really find it difficult to specify who had what in terms of weapons. But they did have some.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to turn your attention to the conditions that existed inside the cell. Firstly, the food. What sort of food did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions were poor. There was a lot of dirt, and the food was poor. They would bring us one or two meals a day, and sometimes no meals at all. They would bring soup, for example. Something had been cooked in it so there was soup left. We would be given that and a piece of corn bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. It was -- the period of time you were in Srebrenica was in winter. What was the temperature like inside the cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was wintertime. How should I know? I know that I was freezing the whole time. So how low below freezing temperature, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was the cell dry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The roof was raining through. The roof leaked. It had given way in some places, so there was rain coming in through the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you told us that when you were in the stable, you became lice-ridden. Did you continue to suffer that condition in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until we were taken to the hospital in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. In the midst of this, did you receive any visits from any officials, Muslim officials? I mean men of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that Zulfo Tursunovic - Zulfo is his first name and Tursunovic is his last name - I remember him coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, first of all, had you ever met this person prior to his arrival at the cell, your prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What did he look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a big man, wearing a moustache, and he had black hair. He was perhaps over 2 metres in height, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What sort of build did he have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was well built, a very sturdy, big man. He was an elderly man, but I do remember him being a very well-built man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you recall how often he came to the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only know that he came this once. I can't say for the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You said that it was Zulfo Tursunovic who came. How do you know it was Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I heard from others that this man was Zulfo Tursunovic, the man the people who were in prison with me knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When he arrived, did he say anything about himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said that we should not worry, that we would all be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did he introduce himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, you said that he told you that you should not worry, and that you would be exchanged. Did any of the inmates say anything to him, for example, "When will we be exchanged?" or anything to that effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. Somebody probably did ask that. I can't vouch for that because I myself was unable to speak, I was in very bad shape. And I don't recall anybody asking that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, earlier in your -- moments ago in your evidence, you described what you could see around the walls, the interior of the cell, and what you could see of the faces and the condition of the men. I'm referring to the blood on the walls, the blood on the floor, the blood on the clothing, the blood on the faces, bruised faces, black eyes, those sorts of matters, those sorts of things. Were those sorts of things present for Mr. Tursunovic to see when he entered the cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He must have seen those things as soon as he entered the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did this utterance that you would be exchanged soon give you any hope?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing: I wouldn't be able to tell you when exactly he came and how much elapsed afterwards, but I do know that exchanges of children did take place, that is, this one child that I heard had been there and some women and this elderly man. So exchanges did take place. Now, how long after his visit did they take place, or maybe they took place before his visit. There were exchanges; I'm not sure whether it was before his visit or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told us of your initial arrival in Srebrenica, at the police station where you were beaten, your transfer to the prison. At any time did -- were you interrogated, asked questions about yourself, your personal background, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Srebrenica. It was the case in Konjevic Polje, but not in Srebrenica. I remember that there were these men who started beating us. Who they were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I want to show the witness a document, if Your Honours please, that will -- may tend to identify him; therefore, we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Registrar, could I give you back P155, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. We're in open session now, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I want to return you now to the issue of your inmates, and I want to ask you what their fate was. You've mentioned their names already. Dragan Ilic, can you recall what ultimately happened to him in the cells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He died in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was it preceded by a beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were beatings being administered, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you see his body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I laid next to him. I was leaning my head against his body at the moment he died. I felt his body go cold. It was all black and blue. His flesh actually changed colour, which was a sign to me that he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What happened to the body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took it away. I have no idea where to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who took it away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. How should I know? People came and took it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You may have mentioned this, and I apologise if I ask you again. About how old was he when he died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was quite young. He could have been between 17 and 20 years of age. I can't be more specific. He was young, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You've told us already that you were infested with lice. Was he infested with lice when he died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You mentioned a man named Kosta. What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from the others in prison that he too had died. It's difficult for me to confirm whether that is true, but that's what I heard in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When did you last see Kosta? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean before the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, no, I mean in the cell. You didn't know him before the war, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm now talking about the cell.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the date or the month. When I arrived, I saw him, but I don't know when this was. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know a man named Mico?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another name that I heard. He was in that room, in a corner. Someone came, a neighbour of his purportedly, who beat him. But I don't know Mico, because he doesn't come from my area. I heard they were from Kravica, but I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What happened to Mico?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he too had died. Whether it's the case or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What about Branko Sekulic? What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Sekulic died. He was together with me in prison, in Cerska. He died, and Dragan Sekulic died too.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Dragan Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do I take it from your answer that Branko died in the cell? Am I correct in that understanding, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he died in the cell at the prison in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: While you were present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What happened to Branko's body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: His body too was taken away. I have no idea where to. It was just taken away, simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who did you receive information from that Mico and Kosta had died? You didn't see them -- your evidence is you didn't actually see them die, as is the case with Dragan and Branko. So who told you that they died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko, I saw him die and I saw them take his body away, but I didn't see the other two. Other people told me that Kosta too had died, but this was something I heard. This wasn't something that I actually saw for myself; therefore, I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But what I'm interested in is this: Who told you, what was your source of information, that Kosta had died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told by those people who were being held in detention there, those elderly people and those other people whom I didn't know by name, those of them who were still alive at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, how would they know if he died? They were locked up with you, so how would they know that Kosta had passed away?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that something this witness can answer? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe they told him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say for sure whether their knowledge of his death was certain. It's something they told me. But whether this information was authentic or not is not something that I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, they did not tell you how they came by that information, whether it was some other inmates who told them that or whether they had actually seen the body being carried out. They never told you how they came to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You've mentioned in your evidence that you had periods of unconsciousness as a result of beatings. Do you know how long you were unconscious for on these occasions? I assume it varied. But were they extended periods of time, or were you unconscious for a matter of minutes, at the most, on each occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to say for how long. I didn't know the date, the month, or the time; therefore, I can't give you an accurate assessment as to how long this lasted each time it happened. I only know that I would lose consciousness and then regain consciousness at some point, but I can't give you any other information on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Earlier you touched upon the topic of you being taken to hospital and, I think, also having something done about the lice from which you suffered. Do you have any recollection of being taken to a hospital in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. We were in the hospital at Srebrenica, but I can't say how many days. I remember they gave us jabs and pills, the doctors did. While we were at the hospital, we were left in peace. No one touched us. We were being treated for a while, after which we were taken back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. I now you can't say how long you were in hospital for, and if you can't answer my question, feel free to say so. But can you tell us if it was a matter of one or two days or a matter of weeks? Can you give us any perspective at all on the sort of -- on the time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about several weeks. I can't specify the number of days either, two, three, four, five, six days. I know that I was there for some time, but I don't believe it was several weeks, not that long.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think we need to go into private session again, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, because of a certain exhibit I want to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I asked you why, I could have anticipated why, but I think the public ought to have some kind of an explanation why we are going into private session needs to have an idea why.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The document will identify this witness, and we can't have that happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, you were, of course, eventually released, and I want you to tell us about that. You've told us the date, or what you believe to be the date, of your release. Can you recall the day that you were released from your prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the date or anything that had to do with it. I only know that when I was admitted to the hospital, that they entered my name into the records there, but I don't know anything else. I just recall that, in general, it was early spring, there wasn't snow around, and that those were the only indications to me of what season it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Who took you away from there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two men who were with me, we heard that the blue helmets had come to pick us up. They were soldiers there at the time, and an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. interpreter. And when they entered the premises, they asked for my name. I told them my name, and then they told me, "You're going with us." They never told me where I was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, the men who told you "You're going with us," were they wearing blue helmets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they had blue helmets, or was it blue berets. I'm not sure. But anyway, there was the UN sign on them, on these helmets or caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were they speaking a foreign language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. I didn't understand the language. They probably spoke English, but I couldn't tell. I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How did you actually physically get out of the cell and out into the open? How did that -- how was that accomplished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreter told me to stand up and go along with them. I was unable to stand up because my feet were swollen, full of fluid. And then somebody went to fetch the stretcher, and as they brought the stretcher, they placed me on it. And then there was this APC that they took me onto, a white APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was that the UN vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably. It was most probably the white APC belonging to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. And where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know where they were taking us. I saw that there were three men with us. I could hear one of them speak, that's what I remember. And two of them were seated next to me, giving me chocolate to eat, but I was unable to. Then, as there was lice crawling all over me, they would be taking them off with their fingers, and they were really appalled at what they saw, the state that I was in. Then I don't know where they were taking me. I know that we were crossing the bridge between Bratunac and Ljubovija. That much I could see from the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you eventually end up in a Serb hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea whether I was in the hospital in Bratunac or not. I only know that there was an ambulance that they were driving me in, and there was this person dressed in a white coat there with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Just tell the Trial Chamber a few things about your physical condition before you went into hospital. Had you lost weight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information gathered in the hospital, because other than that I, for myself, was unable to know these things, I approximately weighed 30 kilos. And I was lice-ridden. That was about what -- the condition I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How much do you weigh now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I weigh about 78 kilos, I believe. I haven't really measured my weight recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Did you -- I'm not asking you whether, in fact, this happened, but did you have any recollection, quite apart from what anyone may have told you, but any recollection of breaking your ribs, of your ribs being broken, when you were in hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aching everywhere, but I do recall this pain in my left side. But other than that, my head, my shoulder blade ached. The pain was all over my body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Obviously, you were treated by doctors in hospital. I just want to run two names past you and see if they -- if you recall them. Dr. Vajka Mitrovic, and a Dr. K. Bogicevic, do you have any recollection or knowledge of those persons? If you don't, it's not a problem. But if you do, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember their names. I might have known them at the time, but I don't remember them now. There was this lady doctor who took care of me, but I really can't remember her name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've got one last document, and we need to go into private session for that, and then we can go back into open session and then I'll complete, I think, before 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a while, please. We have another document that could uncover the identity of the witness. So we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Witness, in all of the time that you were in the stable and in Srebrenica, did anyone ever tell you or explain to you why it was that you had been arrested and were being held in custody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my detention in Cerska, I inquired of some people who came there what the motives or the reason for my arrest were, and the answer they gave me was, "Your lot keeps arresting our lot, so we have to do the same." So I believe that there was no reason, really, except for the fact that I was of a different ethnicity. In my opinion, that was the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you ever informed orally or in writing of any charge, criminal charge, that had been leveled against you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no criminal charges against me. I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Apart from the UN soldiers who you saw on the day of your release, were you ever visited by the Red Cross or given access to any legal representation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any such thing, except for the hospital part that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. We'll continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that seems right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, just to assist the Trial Chamber in its planning, do you think you would be in a position to finish tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think I should be able to take this witness fairly shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. And tomorrow is Friday, isn't it? So there's no point in trying to start with another -- do you intend to start with the next witness again tomorrow or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We don't have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't have one. I would have thought so, I mean, because this was scheduled to last three days in any case, this witness. So we have finished for today, and as soon as we leave this courtroom, you will be escorted out of the courtroom by Madam Usher, and you will return tomorrow. In the meantime, please, may I remind you what I told you yesterday, that between today and tomorrow, you're not to discuss or have contact with anyone in relation to your testimony or the subject matter of your testimony here, okay? I thank you. We'll go out first, then draw down the curtains -- you know what to do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 4th day of February, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.56 a.m.,
